title: Decay: effect of temperature on rate of decay
aim: To investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of fresh milk, by measuring the time taken for the enzyme lipase to lower the pH enough to change the colour of phenolphthalein indicator.
background: Decay is the breakdown of dead organisms and waste by decomposers such as bacteria and fungi. Decomposers release enzymes that digest large molecules into smaller ones. For example, lipase enzymes break down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol. Decay recycles materials such as carbon and mineral ions back into the environment.

Milk contains lipids. When lipase digests the fat in milk, fatty acids are produced, and these lower the pH. In this practical, sodium carbonate solution is added first to make the milk alkaline, and phenolphthalein indicator is added, which is pink in alkaline conditions and colourless below about pH 8.3. The time taken for the pink colour to disappear is a measure of how quickly the lipids are being broken down, which models the rate of decay.

The rate of decay depends on temperature, water and oxygen availability. As temperature increases, enzymes and substrate molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more often, so the rate increases, up to the optimum temperature. Above the optimum the enzyme's active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured, so the rate falls. Rate is calculated as 1 ÷ time.
hypothesis: As temperature increases from 20 °C to about 40 °C, the time taken for the phenolphthalein to turn colourless will decrease (the rate of decay will increase). Above about 40 °C the rate will decrease because lipase is denatured.

variables.independent: Temperature of the water bath (20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C).
variables.dependent: Time taken for the phenolphthalein to change from pink to colourless (s), used to calculate rate (1 ÷ time).
control: Volume of milk (5 cm³), and the same type of milk (full-fat)
Volume and concentration of sodium carbonate solution (7 cm³ of 0.05 mol/dm³)
Volume and concentration of lipase solution (1 cm³ of 5%)
Time allowed for solutions to reach the water bath temperature (10 minutes)
Same method of judging the end point (same person, white background)

equipment: Phenolphthalein indicator in a dropping bottle
Test tubes and test tube rack
Syringes or measuring cylinders for 1 cm³, 5 cm³ and 7 cm³
Electric water baths (or beakers of water with a kettle) at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C
White tile or white paper to view the colour against
method: Label a test tube 'lipase' and use a syringe to add 1 cm³ of lipase solution to it.
Label a second test tube 'milk'. Use a syringe to add 5 drops of phenolphthalein, then 5 cm³ of milk.
Use another syringe to add 7 cm³ of sodium carbonate solution to the milk tube. The solution should turn pink because it is alkaline.
Place a thermometer in the milk tube and put both tubes into a water bath set to 20 °C.
Leave both tubes for 10 minutes so that their contents reach the temperature of the water bath. Check with the thermometer.
Use a clean syringe to transfer 1 cm³ of lipase from the lipase tube into the milk tube and start the stopwatch immediately.
Stir the contents of the milk tube continuously with a glass rod, keeping it in the water bath.
Stop the stopwatch as soon as the solution loses its pink colour, viewing it against a white tile. Record the time in seconds.
If the colour has not changed after 600 seconds, stop and record 'more than 600 s'.
Repeat the whole investigation twice more at each temperature and calculate the mean time.
Calculate the rate of reaction at each temperature using rate = 1 ÷ mean time, and plot a graph of rate against temperature.

safety.risk: Phenolphthalein solution is dissolved in ethanol, which is highly flammable, and phenolphthalein is harmful if swallowed.
safety.precaution: Keep it away from naked flames (use electric water baths), wear eye protection, and wash hands after use.

safety.risk: Enzymes can cause allergic reactions if they get on the skin or are breathed in.
safety.precaution: Avoid skin contact, wipe up spills immediately and wash hands after the practical.
Wear eye protection and wash any splashes off with plenty of water.

safety.risk: Scalds from hot water or hot test tubes.
safety.precaution: Use thermostatically controlled electric water baths, and handle hot test tubes with a test tube holder.

safety.risk: Milk is used with chemicals and could be contaminated; it may go off and grow microorganisms.
safety.precaution: Never drink the milk, use fresh milk and dispose of mixtures down the sink with plenty of water at the end of the lesson.

results.notes: Rate = 1 ÷ mean time, given to 3 significant figures. For example, at 40 °C: 1 ÷ 160 = 0.00625 s⁻¹. At 60 °C the colour did not change within 600 s, so the rate was less than 1 ÷ 600 = 0.00167 s⁻¹. Plot rate (y-axis) against temperature (x-axis) and join the points with a smooth curve.

analysis: As the temperature increased from 20 °C to 40 °C, the mean time for the colour change decreased from 540 s to 160 s, so the rate increased from 0.00185 s⁻¹ to 0.00625 s⁻¹. The rate at 40 °C was about 3.4 times the rate at 20 °C.

Between 20 °C and 40 °C, the lipase and lipid molecules had more kinetic energy as temperature increased, so they moved faster and collided more often. More enzyme-substrate complexes formed, so lipids were broken down into fatty acids more quickly and the pH fell faster.

Above 40 °C the rate decreased: at 50 °C the mean time increased to 280 s, and at 60 °C there was no colour change in 600 s. At high temperatures the bonds holding the lipase in shape break, the active site changes shape and lipids no longer fit. The enzyme is denatured.

The optimum temperature for this lipase is about 40 °C, but it could be anywhere between 30 °C and 50 °C. Testing more temperatures in this range (for example 35, 40 and 45 °C) would find it more precisely.

This models decay in the environment. Decomposers release enzymes such as lipase, so decay is faster in warm conditions and slower in cold conditions. This is why compost heaps decay faster in summer and why food is kept in a fridge to slow decay.

errors.error: Judging when the pink colour has completely disappeared is subjective, and the colour fades gradually.
errors.improvement: Compare with a colour standard (a tube of milk with no sodium carbonate), view against a white tile, have the same person judge every end point, or use a pH probe and data logger to record when pH falls to a set value.

errors.error: The temperature of the mixture may change when the lipase is added or while stirring.
errors.improvement: Warm both solutions in the water bath for the same time before mixing, keep the tube in the water bath throughout, and monitor with a thermometer.

errors.error: Different milks contain different amounts of fat, and milk changes with age.
errors.improvement: Use milk from the same carton, of the same type (full-fat), for every test.

errors.error: Delay between adding the lipase and starting the stopwatch.
errors.improvement: Have one person add the lipase and another start the stopwatch at the same moment.

examTips: Explain the colour change in steps: lipase breaks down lipids into fatty acids (and glycerol), fatty acids lower the pH, phenolphthalein becomes colourless.
Know why sodium carbonate is added: it makes the solution alkaline at the start, so phenolphthalein is pink.

For temperature effects, use kinetic energy and collisions for the rising part of the graph, and denaturation (change in shape of the active site) for the falling part. Never say the enzyme is 'killed'.
Rate = 1 ÷ time. A longer time means a slower rate of decay.
Link the practical to real decay: warm, moist conditions with oxygen speed up decay by decomposers, which is why compost heaps are kept warm and aerated.

questions.question: Why does the colour of the milk mixture change from pink to colourless after lipase is added?
options: Lipase breaks down lipids into fatty acids, which lower the pH
Lipase breaks down proteins into amino acids, which raise the pH
Lipase reacts directly with the phenolphthalein
The milk is heated, which removes the colour
markScheme: 1 mark: lipids are broken down into fatty acids (and glycerol), which lower the pH so phenolphthalein becomes colourless
questions.explanation: Lipase digests lipids, not proteins. The fatty acids produced are acidic, so they lower the pH below the point where phenolphthalein is pink. Lipase does not react with the indicator itself.

questions.question: What is the purpose of adding sodium carbonate solution to the milk at the start?
options: To provide the substrate for lipase
To make the solution alkaline so that phenolphthalein is pink at the start
To denature any enzymes already in the milk
markScheme: 1 mark: to make the solution alkaline (so the indicator starts pink)
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is pink only in alkaline conditions. Sodium carbonate makes the milk alkaline so the change to colourless can be seen as fatty acids are produced. The lipids in milk are the substrate.

questions.question:
At 40 °C the mean time for the colour change was 160 s.
Calculate the rate of reaction using rate = 1 ÷ time. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Rate = 1 ÷ 160 = 0.00625 per second. The unit is s⁻¹ because time was measured in seconds.

questions.question:
At 30 °C, the times for the colour change in three repeats were 290 s, 310 s and 300 s.
Calculate the mean time.
questions.explanation: Add the three times (900 s) and divide by 3 to give 300 s.

questions.question: Explain why the milk tube and the lipase tube are left in the water bath for 10 minutes before they are mixed.
acceptedAnswers: reach the temperature of the water bath
reaction occurs at the correct temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: so that both solutions reach the temperature being tested (of the water bath)
1 mark: so the reaction takes place at that temperature from the start, making the results valid
questions.explanation: If the solutions started at room temperature, the reaction would begin at the wrong temperature and the time would not reflect the temperature being investigated.

questions.question:
Mean times for the colour change were: 20 °C: 540 s; 30 °C: 300 s; 40 °C: 160 s; 50 °C: 280 s.
At which temperature was the rate of decay fastest?
markScheme: 1 mark: 40 °C
questions.explanation: The fastest rate has the shortest time. At 40 °C the colour changed in only 160 s. Choosing 20 °C confuses the longest time with the fastest rate.

questions.question: Explain why the rate of reaction was faster at 30 °C than at 20 °C.
markScheme: 1 mark: at higher temperature the molecules (lipase and lipid) have more kinetic energy / move faster
1 mark: so they collide more often
1 mark: so more enzyme-substrate complexes form and lipids are broken down into fatty acids faster
questions.explanation: Below the optimum, increasing temperature speeds up the reaction by increasing the frequency of collisions between enzyme and substrate.

questions.question: At 60 °C the colour did not change within 600 seconds. Explain why.
acceptedAnswers: lipids no longer fit active site
markScheme: 1 mark: the high temperature changes the shape of the lipase active site (the enzyme is denatured)
1 mark: so the lipid substrate no longer fits the active site
1 mark: so no (or very few) fatty acids are produced and the pH does not fall enough to change the indicator
questions.explanation: Denaturation is a permanent change in the shape of the active site. Avoid saying the enzyme has been 'killed', because enzymes are not alive.

questions.question:
In a compost heap, the mass of a bag of grass cuttings fell from 80 g to 50 g over 6 weeks.
Calculate the mean rate of decay in g per week.
markScheme: 1 mark: mass lost = 80 − 50 = 30 g
1 mark: 30 ÷ 6 = 5 g/week
questions.explanation: Rate of decay = mass lost ÷ time = 30 ÷ 6 = 5 g per week. Dividing the final mass (50 g) by the time would not give the mass that decayed.

questions.question: It is difficult to judge exactly when the pink colour disappears. Suggest two ways to make the end point more accurate.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: view against a white tile; compare with a colour standard of the end colour; the same person judges every end point; use a pH meter or pH probe and data logger to record when the pH reaches a set value
questions.explanation: Colour judgements are subjective. A white background and a reference tube make judgements more consistent, and a pH probe removes the judgement altogether.

questions.question: In natural decay, which organisms release enzymes such as lipase to break down dead material?
options: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi
markScheme: 1 mark: decomposers (bacteria and fungi)
questions.explanation: Decomposers secrete enzymes onto dead material and absorb the small soluble molecules produced. This returns carbon dioxide and mineral ions to the environment.

questions.question: A gardener wants grass cuttings in a compost heap to decay as quickly as possible. Give three conditions that would increase the rate of decay.
markScheme: 1 mark: warm temperature
1 mark: moist (water available)
1 mark: plenty of oxygen (air), for example by turning the heap regularly
questions.explanation: Decomposers need warmth for their enzymes to work quickly, water for their reactions and to absorb food, and oxygen for aerobic respiration.

questions.question:
The mean time for the colour change was 540 s at 20 °C and 160 s at 40 °C.
Calculate how many times faster the rate of reaction was at 40 °C than at 20 °C. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Because rate = 1 ÷ time, the ratio of the rates equals the inverse ratio of the times: 540 ÷ 160 = 3.375, which is 3.4 to 2 significant figures.

questions.question: Describe a method to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of milk, using lipase, sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein.
markScheme: Indicative content: add phenolphthalein (5 drops), milk (5 cm³) and sodium carbonate solution (7 cm³) to a test tube so it turns pink; put lipase (1 cm³) in a separate tube; place both tubes in a water bath at a set temperature; leave to reach that temperature (check with thermometer); add lipase to milk mixture and start stopwatch; stir; stop when pink colour disappears; record time; repeat at a range of temperatures (for example 20 to 60 °C); repeat three times and calculate mean; calculate rate = 1 ÷ time; control volumes and concentrations of milk, lipase, sodium carbonate, number of drops of indicator, white tile for end point

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method that would give valid results, including setting up the pink mixture, temperature control and pre-warming, timing until colourless, a range of temperatures and control variables.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most key steps, but missing detail such as pre-warming, repeats or control variables.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as mixing milk and lipase at different temperatures and timing a colour change, with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: High-scoring answers describe each reagent's role, how temperature is controlled, how the end point is judged and timed, and what is kept the same between temperatures.

questions.question: Use the results of this investigation to explain why food decays more slowly in a fridge (5 °C) than in a warm kitchen (25 °C), and why cooking food at high temperatures can reduce decay.
markScheme: Indicative content: decay is caused by enzymes released by decomposers (bacteria and fungi); at 5 °C molecules have less kinetic energy and collide less often, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and decay is slow; the investigation showed rate increased from 20 °C to 40 °C, so lower temperatures give slower decay; microorganisms also grow and reproduce more slowly in the cold; high temperatures denature enzymes, as shown by no colour change at 60 °C; cooking also kills microorganisms so they cannot cause decay

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains both the effect of low temperature (less kinetic energy, fewer collisions) and high temperature (denaturation of enzymes, killing microorganisms), linked to the results.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that cold slows decay or heat denatures enzymes, with little explanation or use of results.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A strong answer applies both halves of the temperature curve to a real situation and refers to the data, such as the faster rate at 40 °C than at 20 °C and no change at 60 °C.
